utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: He is on his way. (Witness enters court) JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Remind him he is on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you that you are still testifying under oath?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: May we have the appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I am Eric Ostberg. I appear today with Mr Giuliano Turone, Ms Teresa McHenry and our case manager and assistant, Miss Elles van Dusschoten. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: The appearances on the defence side? . MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Good morning, your Honours. I am Edina Residovic, defence counsel for Zejnil Delalic. With me is Professor Eugene O'Sullivan from Canada. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Any other defence appearances?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I do apologise. I was thinking of something else completely. My name is Michael Greaves. I am acting on behalf of Mr Mucic. I have the assistance of Mrs Tapuskovic today. MR. KARABDIC (in interpretation): I am Salih Karabdic. I am defence counsel of Mr Hazim Delic. With me in the team is Mr Thomas Moran from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am John Ackerman on behalf of Esad Landzo. Present in the gallery on his behalf is Mustafa Brackovic. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you very much. I think Ms Residovic is cross-examining. You may wish to continue. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Good morning, your Honours. Good morning, Mr Kuljanin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (In interpretation): Good morning, Madam.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday we were discussing your interrogation by Mr Miroslav Stenek; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr Kuljanin, do you sign your name in Latin alphabet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough, with the help of the usher, to put two signatures on this paper? (Handed)?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder about the relevancy of this experiment. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, we are questioning the witness concerning the statement that he is alleged to have signed. I wish to know how this witness signs his name. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Has he denied signing any statement? MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): I shall continue with the examination, as he denied that he had made other statements. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: If you are pursuing the fact that he has denied signing any statement or making any statement, then perhaps there might be some relevance in making him sign, so that you can cross-check, but without that I think it is unnecessary. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): That is correct. Thank you. Can I ask you then to sign twice in the normal way that you sign things? (Witness signed). Thank you. You said that you had been forced to sign that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that Mr Stenek and the other interrogator asked you about weapons, the military organisation of the defence of Bradina and questions along those lines; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also told me yesterday that in answer to the question whether you had a rifle you had said you had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, under duress.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also confirmed that you were standing before the interrogators for about one hour and that no physical force was used against you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not inside the building, but outside in front of the command building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Asked by the interrogator whether you know anything about the arming of Bradina, you answered at the time, as you say under duress, that you knew that an armoured vehicle had brought automatic rifles from the military barracks in Hadici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had heard that, but I didn't see it, whether there was an armoured vehicle or there were just people there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you told the Commission what you had heard, that such a vehicle had come and that there were 40 rifles inside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must repeat that whatever I said I said under duress. I had to say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were asked whether you were aware of the arming of other people in Bradina, you said at the time, again under duress, as you say, that Zoran Kuljanic (sic) and Radovan Benjo had a mortar, that Boban Simanic also had a mortar, that others had anti-aircraft machine guns, snipers and so on; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is true that I said that under duress.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were also asked about the military organisation in Bradina; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time you said that the commanders in Bradina were --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry. The names? Would you please repeat the names?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That the defence was under the leadership of Rajko Dordic. Is that the Rajko Dordic of whom you said yesterday that he had been working in the Territorial Defence of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr Kuljanin, is that the same Rajko Dordic who told you to go back with Drasko Koprivica when he was wounded during your attempt to cross over into Serb-held territories?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, Mr Kuljanin, after this interrogation were you interrogated again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the SUP of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell me who interrogated you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us when you were interrogated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr Kuljanin, while you were in Musala, were you interrogated by a commission headed by Madam Jasna Dzuhmur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you sign a record of that interrogation while you were in Musala?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will show you a report for you to verify whether this is your signature. Will you also help me, Mr Usher, to give a copy to the Prosecution and the members of the Trial Chamber? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I hope counsel appreciates the contention of the witness that it was done under duress. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, this is a different statement that the witness says he never made, and it was taken seven months after the first statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I made that statement in SUP. I did not say that I had not made it. I said that I made it in SUP, Konjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please look at it? Is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I did not follow what SUP is. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): The police, your Honour. It is the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: SUP? MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): MUP. One is the Ministry of Internal Affairs; the other is the Secretariat of Internal Affairs. Before it was called the Secretariat of Internal Affairs. Later the name was changed to the Ministry of Internal Affairs. SUP is the acronym for the first and MUP for the second name. Mr Kuljanin, have you looked? Is what you stated during that interrogation correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr Kuljanin, you do not recall the correctness of the statement that you made. Therefore, Mr Kuljanin, it is possible that that statement is correct, only you do not remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It may not be correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also do not recall exactly because of your previous experiences in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That I can never forget. What I went through in Celebici I can never forget.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell me whether this is your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. For the record, please let us note that in the statement of January 23rd 1993 he identified his signature and thereby this document, and I tender it as evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was not a legal court in Konjic, at least not for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr Kuljanin, will you please answer whether yesterday, asked by my learned colleague, the Prosecutor, you said that you were not the subject of any court proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true. I do not remember having been sentenced in any way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true what you say today, that you did make a statement before the police, contrary to what you said yesterday in answer to my learned colleague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't know what police that was, what law it stood for, who it represented.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr Kuljanin. That police was working in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but at that time any shepherd even could have questioned me. Anyone could pick me up and take me to the SUP to question me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should like to ask a representative of the Registry to give me the number of the exhibit, please, that we have tendered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is no evidence, madam. Let me say that again. I had to put down whatever I had to. I didn't make a single statement voluntarily. Everything was made under duress.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honours, will you please caution the witness to answer my questions, and I haven't put a single question to him yet?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is number D/19. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I do not know. What are you tendering it for? What are you tendering this other statement for? What are you tendering it for?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Because the witness stated that he made this statement, that he signed this statement, and because the defence will be establishing the facts which are contained in this statement. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: But you do not tender a statement which is contested not to be voluntary except you establish its voluntariness. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, the witness recognised as a statement that he made in the police and which he signed. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes, he said so, but he stated it was under duress. If you want, that statement has to be tried to determine whether it was under duress or not. That is a preliminary issue in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: At this stage you only want to show that this document bears his signatures. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: No, that is not what she said. She said she wanted to tender it as a statement he made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The statement bears his signatures. That is all you want.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, your Honour, please. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Yes. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: If he was denying he never made a statement, then the issue whether it was voluntary or not would not have come in, but the moment he contested the voluntariness, it is in issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to join in the tender of the exhibit with my learned colleague. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: It will not make any difference to my views.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to suggest to the court that it may be admissible for a limited purpose, that being admissible as a document bearing upon the credibility of this witness, and therefore it may be considered by the court for the relevancy it has regarding his credibility and only that and not the -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: This is more than an issue of credibility. When the voluntariness is in issue, it is a matter which should be tried and determined, whether it was made voluntarily or not. It is not enough merely to challenge it for credibility's sake. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, I suggest that we note that this is a document on which the witness recognised his signature and the defence will tender it as an exhibit in the later course of the proceedings. Can we accept the identification of the document only in that way? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: If he is not denying that he signed this document. He has never denied that. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): So it is simply a document submitted for the identification of the signature. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I said the witness is not denying that he signed the document. He is not denying that. He is only telling you that he did not do that voluntarily. You do not put in any statement made not voluntarily. This is quite beyond the experience I have. The procedure for doing that is very clear. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honour -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I do not see any business for its admission, not one. Even for identification, identification for what? A statement which has already been denied as not being voluntary? MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Every common lawyer who is perhaps on your side knows the procedure for treating such a matter. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you, your Honours. I can simply say that the witness recognised his signature on this document, because, as you have said, I am not able to use this exhibit for other purposes, and the defence will refer to it later on in the submission of evidence. Mr Kuljanin, let us go back to some other questions, which you probably have some knowledge of. Will you tell me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Excuse me. How will you later on refer to this document unless we know there is a paper on which his signatures exist? How will we refer to this document later on unless there is some sort of marking on this document showing that this is a document on which he admits his signatures? How will you refer to it later on? MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, I did suggest that this document be identified as a document whose signature the witness recognised. There are other signatures on this document, and the defence will be able to call up persons who had taken this statement. In answer to my question, the witness said that he had never made a statement before this Commission. Later on he admitted but under duress. That is why the court has not admitted the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't say that I didn't make it. I said that I didn't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But when you saw the document, you recalled that you had made a statement before this Commission. You also remembered that this was your signature, although I had denied it before. For these reasons, as a question of credibility of this witness, I had suggested that this document be accepted for these limited purposes. The Trial Chamber did not agree. I can repeat my proposal, but I think that the decision of the Trial Chamber is clear. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: The overriding interests which is a matter of admissibility is based on the voluntariness of the statement. All you are trying to show is that a particular document was signed by him, which is a prelude to actually saying it is a statement made by him. You do not go about things that way. If a question of voluntariness is in issue, you try that voluntariness and satisfy the Trial Chamber that it was made voluntarily. Then it will be admitted. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): In answer, your Honours, to this question, since there are five other signatures on this document, I will offer it later into evidence as a Defence Exhibit. Thank you, Mr Kuljanin. You also know Gojko Dordic and Ranko Zivak, your neighbours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zivak Ranko, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Gojko Dordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know Sreten Zelenovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know that Sreten Zelenovic was a butcher in Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he had a butcher's shop and cafe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: His shop was near the highway?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For a while, Mr Kuljanin, you worked for Mr Zelenovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr Kuljanin, your father is Stevan and he is an auto mechanic; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that he was a popular person in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was repairing cars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that his nickname was "Vojvoda Vodnik"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was "Voda"; in translation "leader".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he write and perform songs about Serbian national heroes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that is not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr Kuljanin, let me go back to something I had asked you a little while ago relating to the statement that you gave. Did you state to the Commission, when asked this question, that you turned in your rifle because there was some suspicion that you had stolen some metal armature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which Commission is this?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true, Mr Kuljanin, that you stopped working for Sreten Zelenovic because he suspected that you stole meat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I stopped working because there was no work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one more question, Mr Kuljanin. Did you in April or May belong to the Army of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you did not, and you were not a member of any other military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a member of the JNA. I was there in 1991/92.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I mean in that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you did not respond to the mobilisation of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not called up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that it was forbidden by the military authorities to leave the area of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr Kuljanin, I would like to ask you again: Did you personally acquire any weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you turn in your weapons to MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr Kuljanin. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, just for the sake of clarity, that statement was not tendered as evidence, but it has been marked for identification; is that correct? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Which statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The one about which we were discussing. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: No, it was not marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: There is a distinction, is there not, between marking it for identification and having it entered as evidence. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: That was not the application, was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, you refused to enter it as evidence, but it has -- I am asking whether it has been marked, which is a different issue altogether. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: If there was an application for identification, obviously it could be. He identified his signature. All right. It can be identified. It cannot be tendered as his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes. Can we be told the number that statement has, please? How have you marked that statement for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is document number D/19A Cross-examination by MR. ACKERMAN JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Good morning, Mr Kuljanin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My name is John Ackerman. I represent Esad Landzo before the Tribunal. I have, I think, just a very few questions that I want to ask you this morning; okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You recall, do you not, that in April of 1992, while you were living in Bradina, that the traffic between Sarajevo and Konjic was interrupted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And actually there are tunnels at either end of Bradina where the road was blocked and checkpoints were set up; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were no barricades, but the Muslim army put mines on both ends. One was by the Muslim army and the other one by the local Muslims from the villages of Zukici and others, but there were no barricades, and I don't remember them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember a checkpoint that was in Bradina itself near Mico's coffee shop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That was not -- the cafe was not in the centre of Bradina and there was no checkpoint by the Mico restaurant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do know that some of the residents of Bradina at least had been receiving arms from either the SDS or the JNA prior to the attack on Bradina in May of 1992? You know that, do you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Although you have told this Tribunal that you did not participate in the defence of Bradina in any way, other inhabitants of Bradina were involved in the defence and actually fired weapons in the course of the war that went on in Bradina for a couple of days; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know that anybody fired from the village of Bradina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you if you know a person by the name of Almir Padalovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know him by sight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know that at one point in time this person was a guard at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes for a period of time, not very long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know then that there came a time that he left there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know when he left. I don't know when he left. I was not a camp commander to know which guard left camp at what time. Only guards who wanted to beat people were there. Those who did not, they were not there. I don't know when he left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why he left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How could I? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that he became quite distraught and did you not see him crying after Zjelko Klimenta had been shot, saying that it was his fault and that it was an accidental shooting? Do you not remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember him crying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you said, I think maybe in your prior testimony, that while you were in Hangar Number 6 that the guards never would enter the hangar during the night-time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the night-time? Sometimes they did. Not very often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You knew, while you were in Celebici, did you not, that Konjic was being shelled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You could not hear the shelling of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did hear, but I did not see. For you something is worth only if it's seen, not if it's heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I agree with you about that. There came a time when you were transferred to Musala prison, I think on November 17th, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see Esad Landzo, Zenga, at Musala prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe two times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Inside or outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once, one time I saw him inside, and one time I saw him outside. For a while he was detained together with Delic with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to talk to you now about the prisoner Zjelko Cecez. Do you remember that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have testified that that person was called out of Hangar 6 by Zenga; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know who called him out. It was dark. It was 1 o'clock in the morning. He was called out and taken out. He was beaten. I heard moans. I did not see it. I heard Zjelko's moans. Four prisoners were then called out to carry him in, and then in the morning and when I woke up he was dead. He was lying close to me and he remained there for two days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you have no knowledge, as you sit here today, as to either who called him out or who beat him; do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I don't know. It was dark.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With regard to the prisoner Bosko Samoukovic you have previously said that that beating also took place outside and you wouldn't have been able to observe that either; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I only saw two blows, which he received from Esad Landzo inside the hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you don't know who administered blows outside the hangar, but you do know that he was beaten outside the hangar; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know if he was being hit behind the hangar, because I know that he was hit in there with the plank, and then later he was taken to the infirmary, where he died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You certainly cannot tell this Tribunal, can you, that he was not beaten after he was removed from the hangar, can you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told the Tribunal at the beginning of your testimony that there were three occasions while you were at Celebici where you were beaten in a manner that you characterised as cruelly, bad beatings; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have told us that the first of those was the day you arrived at the camp, on May 27th 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That the second of those was the day that the International Red Cross came, August 12th 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the third of those was just before you were transferred to Musala on November 17th 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that there was one time when Esad Landzo kicked you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, in relation to those three severe beatings you have talked about, when that happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us any kind of an estimate? Was it close to the time you arrived or close to the time you left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was June, July, somewhere around there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Could I ask the assistance of the Registrar in putting Prosecution Photo Number 30 that we were referring to yesterday or the day before onto the ELMO, so I can have the witness take a look at it, please? (Handed). Do you now see that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that Hangar 6 that you were confined in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly that it is Hangar Number 6, because there were a number of hangars. It wasn't just one like this, because there's no number here, but it is a hangar, but I don't know if it's Number 6.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it like Hangar 6? Does it look like Hangar 6 to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Assuming for the purposes of your testimony that it is Hangar 6, and I can tell you that it has been so identified, could you take a pointer and to the extent you can, show the Tribunal the three places that you were seated inside Hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Pointing).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me the number of the spot as you point to it. Are you pointing to number one now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is number one and the other two positions I cannot see here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because they would be against that other wall; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct. Against that wall that you cannot even see here (pointing).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like you to pay attention to the windows in that photograph. Are they the same as they were when you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think they are the same, but you couldn't see through those windows at all. They were dirty. I don't know. You couldn't see through them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at the floor for me and tell me if the floor looks the same?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were sitting in that hangar in positions 2 and 3 that you have described, were you able to look out the opposite windows on the other side of the hangar and see anything going on outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those windows were not like these windows there. Those windows were not open. Maybe they were open about twice during my stay in the hangar. From position number one, where I sat, I could not see anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about from position 2 or 3? Could you see through those windows what was going on outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From position number 2 I also -- I cannot remember seeing anything at all. From position number 3 I also did not see anything. I don't remember seeing anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any trucks going by outside through those windows?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not. I heard, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like the usher to assist me in showing the witness a couple of photographs which I have previously showed to the Prosecutor. (Handed) what number is it that is on that document, Mr Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is number D7/4.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr Kuljanin, I am showing you a couple of photographs that have been marked D7/4. My question to you is: Do you recognise anyone in either of those photographs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you point to the person that you have identified as Esad Landzo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are pointing to the second person from the left in the photograph that is black and white; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because he is the only man there, and I pointed at him in camouflage uniform, and the other one is his brother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The photograph on the right, the colour photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which person in that photograph have you identified as his brother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first person here. I think it's his brother, because they look similar. They look quite alike. This photograph where he is wearing a camouflage uniform is not very clear to me, so I cannot identify fully. I don't know if it's him or his brother. I'm not going to say for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have been informed that there may be some mix-up in the identification of that document. Could I ask the Registrar to repeat that, so I'm certain for the record at least what the identification number is?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For the large photograph the number is D7/4 and for the small one in colour the number is D7(a)/4.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honour, I would offer those photographs D7/4, D7(a)/4 as photographs that have been identified by this witness and for the persons that he has identified within them. I think the Prosecution has no objection; is that correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. So will they be admitted then, your Honour? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: For identification, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And admitted as exhibits in the case; correct? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: What exhibit is this? What is it for?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you looking for a reason why they should be? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In the first place they have been offered and the prosecution has not objected to their admission, so it is by agreement that they are being admitted. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I should understand why it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In the second place I would suggest to you that they are relevant for a number of reasons. They will become additionally relevant with other witnesses that will testify in the case, but as this witness has told you, Esad Landzo and his brother look very much alike, and that it's very, very difficult for him to distinguish between the two of them, and he even took the position that he did not want to say for certain that the person depicted in the black and white left-hand photo was Esad Landzo, that it could have been his brother. Much of the testimony that this Chamber has heard and will be hearing throughout this case involves persons identifying Mr Esad Landzo as having done certain things. To the extent that those identifications took place at a place other than Celebici, there is the possibility that the witnesses are confusing he and his brother. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Actually this is the first issue of mistaken identity I have heard since we started.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It may have been confused in the picture, but not in Celebici. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: No one has ever suggested that. Perhaps you are introducing it for the first time. That is why I want to be informed why you really want to. I now hear why you want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: If I may remind your Honour, although we did not object to the admission of these photographs, there is anyway already in our transcript a stipulation to the identification of Mr Landzo in this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I fully understand that, your Honour. I'm talking about matters -- I'm sure that the stipulation is with regard to whether or not he was a guard at Celebici. I have no problem with that. I am referring to other misidentification that may have taken place outside Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: The stipulation we had does not concern only the quality or the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I am certain there is no stipulation before this court that every time a witness identifies Esad Landzo that we have stipulated that that identification is correct. I'm quite certain we have not done that. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Do not be mistaken. I am not fishing at all. I just wanted the Trial Chamber to be sure exactly why those pictures were going in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Then I think this matter is at rest and I can go on. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Mr Kuljanin, you had told the Trial Chamber in your direct testimony that there came a time when all of your belongings were taken from you; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would those have consisted of? What was taken from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How can I remember? How do I know? Everything was taken away from me. Whatever I had was taken away from me. I don't remember what I had on me. I don't understand these questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So even though it's your testimony that things were taken from you, you have no idea what those things were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no idea. How could I know? I had some money. I had something in gold. I had my clothes. Everything was taken away. I had new clothes. I had two jackets that were taken away from me. The fighters of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, they didn't have what to wear, so they took my two jackets and put them on. What kind of army is that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So a moment ago you said you couldn't remember what was taken from you and now you have described two jackets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have described.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some gold?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because you repeated the question. That's why I'm explaining it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some gold was taken from you. What kind of gold?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. A chain and a ring. Do you want me to tell you how many grams it weighed?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really can't remember. I really don't know how many grams I had in gold. That's rather funny.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What else was taken from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My house. My house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about having been taken from your person, things you were carrying on your person. What was taken from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two jackets, tee-shirts, gold and documents, my personal documents. I don't know what else I had by way of documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those things were all taken at the time of your arrest in Bradina; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, in Celebici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the BH soldiers took the jackets from you in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The BH soldiers took the gold from you in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Croatian Defence Council, HVO. How do I know who it was exactly?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the personal documents were taken from you in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By BH soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. When you were near the end of the examination of the Prosecutor yesterday you were asked a question, and your response to the question was that you could not know because when you were in Hangar Number 6 you were forced to sit with your head down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depended on the guard. Mostly we did have to look down at the ground, but what we were interested in, we saw. What we were not interested in we couldn't be bothered to look.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you demonstrate for the Tribunal, just seated there in your chair, the posture that you would be in and that you were required to be in when you had your head down? Show us what that would look like, if you can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot. I'm sitting on a chair. I was sitting on the ground in Celebici. I can't explain it to you sitting on a chair.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may he be permitted to leave the witness chair and sit on the ground so we can see the manner in which he was forced to sit at Celebici? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Do you think that is really necessary, for him to repeat that exercise?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't know that it has ever been done in this court, your Honour. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: It is not even necessary to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it is very difficult for us to understand what these prisoners could have seen if we can't get a graphic -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: We are even not in that environment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I am sorry. I did not understand your last -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: We are not even in that environment for him to simulate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What does the witness mean: "not Celebici"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We're not in Celebici now, so that I can explain. You are reminding me of 1992. That was in 1992. If I sit down there, it's as if we're back in 1992. I'm going through the whole experience again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you are telling me again is that would be painful for you to have to repeat that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It would be painful, and I would recall everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then I will not ask you to do it. You have told us --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr Kuljanin, on many occasions you have answered questions of all of the examiners, including the Prosecutor, with the response: "I don't remember", and at one point you suggested that because of your confinement and the treatment you received during this war time that your memory is somewhat faulty. Is that a fair characterisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. My memory is not 100 per cent well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe that's all I have, your Honours. Thank you. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you very much. Any re-examination? Re-examination by MR. TURONE

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Just two questions, your Honour, in re-examination. We would like to go back for a moment, Mr Kuljanin, to the document which was shown to you by Ms Residovic, the one containing a signature and dated January 1993, the SUP document, let us say. Do you remember in that occasion how many people were there present belonging to the police and questioning you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember, your Honours. Any statement that I signed -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I am not sure this arose out of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: This is stemming from the cross-examination. I wanted just to clarify the number of the people, police people, present in that situation. He says he does not remember anyway. So my second question concerns again the photo number 30, the hangar photo number 30, and I would like this photo number 30 of Exhibit Number 1 to be put on the ELMO again for the witness, please, by the usher. (Handed). Now, Mr Kuljanin, do you see this photo again? Do you see right on the left side, the extreme left side of this photo, on the floor on the extreme side of the photo, do you see a kind of a dark line going along the wall? Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say what is this line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a kind of canal, a kind of canal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that a covered canal with something or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were some rails on top, like railings and below there was a canal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. This concludes my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Does this arise out of cross-examination, this question which you have just put? I thought it arose out of cross-examination from the last witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: This is also coming from the cross-examination of Mr Ackerman, who wanted to show this photo to the witness. Mr Ackerman asked for particular details about the floor and this is why I wanted to get through this open door. This concludes my re-examination, your Honour. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: That is all for this witness, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Okay. You are discharged now. This is all for you. Thank you very much for your assistance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too, sirs. (Witness withdrew) JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Now who is your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, our next witness would be Miss Sabine Manke, who was an investigator with the Office of the Prosecutor. It would be the witness by which we would seek to introduce the statements of the accused. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: That puts us in some difficulties, because you know there is already a motion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. If you wanted to hear legal argument before she was called, that would be fine with us. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I think we will proceed with hearing her. At the relevant point when you want to tell her the question, I think the precautions necessary for taking these statements will be an issue. So we will hear argument at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I will just point out maybe, in anticipation of the defence, that with respect to the statements there are, I believe, two, maybe now with something filed yesterday by the defence of Landzo really three, issues. The one issue brought by the defence counsel of Mr Delalic, brought by Mme Residovic, concerns specifics in the exact manner the interview was taken, and I think your Honour is correct that it is appropriate to hear the witness about that issue. With respect to the other issues, all the defence counsel have stipulated as to the authenticity of the recordings and the transcripts and so I don't believe, although this witness -- I may ask her just "what are these?"; and she would say "the tape recordings" or "the transcripts". All the defence counsel have agreed to that. The only issue is going to be the legal issue which arises as to the mention in some of the statements of the co-accused. So if your Honours wanted to hear that particular legal issue first, as I understand it, it is not necessary to hear that witness, because, in fact, all the defence counsel have agreed that the tape recordings and the transcripts -- that the recordings are the correct and authentic transcripts of -- I am sorry -- recordings of what occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, your Honour. A couple of things. First, I don't recall entering in such a stipulation. I asked my lead counsel and he doesn't recall. He may have and I may have and we just don't recall T secondly, based on a ruling from the court earlier this morning on voluntariness, we will be filing either today or tomorrow a request for a hearing based on the voluntariness of Mr Delic's waiver of his right to silence due to some cultural differences on the effect of making a statement. I believe I will have either one or two affidavits attached to that on the voluntariness of that waiver. This may require a hearing with some witnesses before the Trial Chamber. That again is based on the Trial Chamber's Ruling with the last witness and his statement on voluntariness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Would it not be better you reserve objection until we have heard the person who is producing that statement. Maybe the witness can say -- can describe the circumstances under which that statement was recorded?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, Judge Jan, the issue is -- what goes to voluntariness is this. I have been informed by my Bosnian colleagues that the practice in the former Yugoslavia and in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina is that a statement made to an investigating police officer has a very distinct difference and very, very limited admissibility in a later trial, and therefore it would go to the understanding of what the effect of making such a statement is, and that would in turn go to the voluntariness of the waiver of the right to silence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But we will just be talking in abstract terms. Let us first of all find out the circumstances under which the statement was recorded, the assurances of voluntariness given by the person recording the statement, the circumstances where the statement was recorded. Unless we have all these facts, it is very difficult to answer the question which you are raising in the abstract.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I understand. By the way, there is no allegation that we are making that anybody used thumbscrews or anything like that to get a statement out of Mr Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Let us have the full picture about the circumstances in which that statement was recorded. That can only come after we hear the person who recorded the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is fine, your Honour. I will be filing something this afternoon or tomorrow morning probably with some affidavits attached. Thank you very much, judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, before this witness gives evidence, there is a motion before the court to the effect that the prosecution have not complied with Rule 66(a) in this court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is again a question of fact, whether it has been complied with or not. That will again be a question of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: This goes to the heart of whether this Tribunal is going to allow this witness to give evidence or not. The prosecution have not supplied any notice of what evidence this witness is to give. They have supplied notice of the exhibits that this witness is to produce but not the evidence which that witness is to give. The motion that was filed on Monday by all counsel goes to the very heart of the spirit of the laws that this Tribunal -- and the Rules that this Tribunal operates under. I would draw your Honour's attention to the motion that was filed and the argument that is set out there for saying why the prosecution should be prevented from calling this witness. They have failed to honour both in the spirit and in the letter the rules set out by the Tribunal, Rule 66(a), which requires them to give notice of the evidence which their witnesses give, in my submission. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Can we hear Miss McHenry? Let us hear your reaction to Mr Greaves's argument.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: First my reaction to Mr Greaves's argument is we have fully complied with Rule 66(a). We have given copies of absolutely everything. I find this frankly incredible. All I can think about is that they are making an argument that somehow, because this witness has not made a witness statement, that somehow she cannot testify. I think there is, first of all, absolutely nothing in the Rules which would require the prosecution to make sure that every witness provide a witness statement. I will also point out that they have been told months and months ago that we would introduce all the statements into evidence, and that is why this witness has been called. If there is any doubt about what a witness is going to testify about, either with respect to this witness or in the future, the defence is free to ask us. If there is any confusion, but in particular with respect to this witness, it has been told to all defence counsel, and I do not believe that there can be any representation made in good faith that they did not know that this witness was going to testify about the introduction of the statements. It is also the case, just to be clear -- I have been handed our initial witness list, and it was said, for instance, Miss Manke may testify, if necessary, on chain of custody issues or explanations on how given evidence was obtained. So I find Mr Greaves's argument totally unfounded. I will also just mention with respect to Mr Moran, although I do not believe that it will necessarily affect our proceedings, that if the accused seek to exclude evidence obtained from them, including statements, they are required to do this well prior to trial. That is an explicit rule and it is to ensure that these long hearings don't occur. It is the case that all the accused, and, in fact, one accused did -- Ms Residovic did bring a motion under Rule 73, in which, in fact, she raised some of the exact legal arguments that Mr Moran seeks to raise, which has to do with the proceeding in Bosnia and what may or may not have been done, around whether or not strict compliance with the Rules of Evidence -- whether that was enough, and the Trial Chamber explicitly found that by following the Rules, Rules 42 and 43, the legal arguments were not valid. So I would also, although we can wait to argue those -- I would certainly object to any attempt at this late hour to challenge such -- the admission of these statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, in response, Rule 73(c) -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Please let me first hear Mr Greaves, whether there are any outstanding documents which you expect from the prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes, indeed there are an awful lot.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I am sorry. My fingers didn't get it. There are a substantial number of items that the prosecution have indicated they will not call witnesses and a substantial number of statements which are simply not -- we have no notice at all of what these witnesses are going to say. Can I remind your Honour of this, and I see that Judge Jan has a copy of the very helpful Green Book we have which we use. Article 21(4)(b) of the Statute: "In determination of any charge against the accused pursuant to the present Statute the accused shall be entitled to the following minimum guarantees in full equality: (b) to have adequate time and facilities for the preparation of his defence and to communicate with counsel of his own choosing." It is an essential feature of any just and fair system of law that the prosecution shall provide to the defence notice of the evidence which they intend to call. They have given us no notice whatsoever of the evidence that this witness intends to give. How are we to prepare our defence in those circumstances? Are we to guess at it, look in a crystal ball, look for fairies at the bottom of the garden to tell us? How may we know, if they do not serve evidence upon us, not exhibits? . The copies of transcripts are exhibits. I am talking about evidence. How are we to prepare our case if the prosecution does not even bother to give us notice of what their case is? . That is what I say. That is why I say there has been a substantial, serious and unjust breach of the Article of the Statute. In my submission what they have done is utterly unfair. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Actually, if I understand you correctly, you expect this witness to have made a statement of what the witness is coming to say today.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: That is precisely it. They refer in their witness list to dealing with issues of continuity, so on and so forth. How are we to know what the evidence is, if we are to meet and challenge it, if we so wish? That is the question I pose. In my submission my learned friend's dismissal of this argument does the prosecution no credit whatsoever. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Let us hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Just very quickly in response to the argument from Ms McHenry that this is an untimely request on our part, Rule 73(c) says: "The Trial Chamber may grant relief upon a showing of good cause." Our position is that the good cause is the Trial Chamber's Ruling today, not 30 minutes ago, on voluntariness of statements and admissibility of statements, and that is our good cause, judge. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Actually we are not arguing the question of your waiver at this stage, I think. If we were arguing that, we would have known exactly what constitutes good cause for your lateness in applying. The good cause is why you have been late in applying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the application becomes -- based on the Trial Chamber's Ruling this morning is what makes the application in our submission a good application. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: It is an application which should have been made long before now. It is what you are now relying on, a subsequent Ruling, as a good cause. As I said, we are not talking about that at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is fine, your Honour. I understand what you are saying. Thank you very much. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes, Ms McHenry. I thought all counsel is contending is that they know nothing about what this witness is coming to say?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that is, one, incorrect. Two, I mean, I have already stated what has been in there, and this defence counsel themselves have indicated that they believe that this next witness is going to testify about the statements. I believe, in fact, that has been said in court, but I will point out there is absolutely nothing in the Rules which requires that every witness give a witness statement. To the extent that the defence thinks that there is any confusion, it would be one thing if we sort of refused to make it, but we are not required to make every single witness give a witness statement. Of course, we are not supposed to confuse them or something else. We have acted in entirely good faith. Defence counsel has known, and if there was any question in their mind, any real question, as opposed to playing games to try to not get things in, they could have enquired of us. In fact, I do not believe there is anything in the Rules which requires that we spell out for them in detail every possible thing that a witness might testify to. In fact, I believe that your Honours have already indicated that it is not the case that every witness must give a witness statement. So I believe these arguments are entirely not valid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will not accept the allegation by Ms McHenry that at least what I am doing is playing games and I do not think any defence counsel is playing games and I resent that. The motion that I filed with this court yesterday --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Hear! Hear!

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- asks this court under Rule 73(c) for good cause to extend the time for a filing of the motion to suppress the statement of Esad Landzo. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Actually the motion is not before us here. It is not before us now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't know where it is. It has been filed, but it seems to me -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes, but it is not before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It seems to me it has to be determined before the witness after the witness that is being called comes to the witness statement. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: You are speaking about a motion which is not before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I am suggesting to your Honours it must be brought to the Trial Chamber before the witness after the one the Prosecution is calling now is permitted to testify. I think I have a right to have it heard. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: The accused person has the right to be heard, whatever the problems are. He has a right to be heard, but it has to be heard according to the schedule of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I fully understand that, and I am not arguing with the schedule of the Trial Chamber. What I am suggesting to your Honours, the second witness that the Prosecution intends to call regarding these would be the witness through which the statement of Esad Landzo would be admitted. If I am requesting an opportunity to challenge the admissibility of that statement and move to suppress it, it would seem to me that motion would have to be heard before the court admitted it, or it is of no moment whatsoever. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Well, I suppose when you might have scaled the hurdle of being properly before the Trial Chamber, then it will be heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. MS. TAPUSKOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, the defence of Mr Mucic has submitted two motions linked to this problem and in the hearing of the 23rd April my learned colleague McHenry spoke about this problem and referred exclusively to Article 73(c). That Rule is not questioned by Mr Mucic's defence counsel. We are simply saying that other Rules from the Rules of Evidence and Procedure were not respected when the statements were taken. For those reasons, since the prosecution now intends to bring witnesses who were present, officials of the Office of the Prosecution who were present when the statements were made, we have transcripts from which it can be seen that the rules laid down were not respected. That is why we are asking that those witnesses not be heard before we have a Ruling on legal matters regarding the method in which those statements were taken. This does not only apply to Sabine Manke. I agree with colleague Ackerman. Another witness is due to appear who was present when the accused Landzo was making a statement. The witness following that was present when Mr Mucic gave his statement. Therefore, according to the transcript that we received, we see that the procedure was not respected and that is why we oppose that this way of introducing evidence be accepted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just a minute. By providing the witness list to the defence did you indicate against this particular witness that she will be proving the statements earlier made by the accused?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No, your Honour, we did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You should have.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Had anyone -- we have, in fact, told the defence counsel that within the last several weeks, and that is, in fact, why -- and they, in fact, said: "Could you put it back a little bit?" We did put it back a little bit. There has been no hiding the fact that we were going to get the statements in and that we were going to do it through an OTP investigator, and that within the last month we have told the defence counsel that we are going to call an OTP investigator, and we gave them the name, about this. It was not in the initial witness list, because at that time we thought that they still may agree to it, that they might agree that a witness was not even necessary, but, your Honour, there is nothing in the Rules that requires us to be that specific, particularly when they have made no effort to, in fact, even ask us. This is the first -- I mean, other than the motion, which was so vague that we didn't even know exactly what was being referred to; other than the motion filed by Mr Greaves yesterday, this is the first we have heard about it. If they would like to sort of request something else, they can, but with respect to these witnesses it has been told to defence counsel, even if it was not in the initial witness statement, that these witnesses are going to testify about the statements. In fact, that is why for the last three weeks defence counsel have, in fact, said: "Your Honour, the prosecution is going to call several witnesses in the near future to get these statements in." We gave them their names. I do not believe that there can be any question that this is -- this -- that this is what they are going to refer to. In fact, there is nothing -- the accused have had the statements for months and months and months. In fact, each accused got their statement immediately after having given it. They get a copy of it in a transcript. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you very much. We will come back at noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can I just give you have some further information, your Honour, so that you can make a proper decision. I don't know if you have seen the witness list. Have you seen that document?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: It was filed with the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can I just refer you to the phraseology that is used against the name of this particular witness: "OTP investigator, if necessary, on a chain of custody issues". These are the important words: "Or explanations on how given evidence was obtained". Can I remind your Honours of Rule 95 and Rule 89. One of the provisions which this court, I think, holds dear to itself: "No evidence should be admissible if obtained by methods which cast substantial doubt on its reliability or if its admission is antithetical to and would seriously damage the integrity of the proceedings." I stress the word there "obtained." The prosecution says that they are not obliged to give us any indication of how this evidence was obtained. In my submission, if we are to exercise our rights under Rule 95 and Rule 89, we are entitled to notice of those issues. If we cannot do that, we shall be asking for an adjournment so that we can properly prepare our case. That is what the damage is that is going to be done, that the court is going to have its time wasted if the Prosecution do not comply with the rules. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you very much, Mr Greaves. What I have heard from all the arguments, I suppose the moment the witness gets on to the stand you might be able to stop putting it to her. We will come back at 12. (11.35 am) (Short break) (12.00 noon) KARIBI WHYTE: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. We have considered the arguments. The Trial Chamber is of the view that we can carry on except the defence thinks that it is impossible that they can follow the arguments, but I think we can carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is one other motion that was filed with you, which you have, which was not discussed before the break, and that is the motion by the defendant Delalic requesting a hearing to exclude evidence. In that regard -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Actually we have not discussed any motions today.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The motion is before you, your Honour. It is entirely directed to the next witness. That is why I wish to address it now and have your -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: When was that filed?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yesterday. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Do you know anything about this? Professor O'Sullivan, I have just seen it. I think it must have been lying on my table. I did not notice it. We can take the arguments any time it becomes relevant. We can take it. I said we can take up arguments on your motion any time it becomes relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I submit the time is relevant. Now is the time to deal with this. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I have not said that. We will start with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it will be too late if the witness is heard. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Why not? Because the objections you are raising there will arise before the witness. Unless the witness is called, it may not be able to go forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Apart from that, Professor O'Sullivan, if at any stage we find that the safeguards which are there for the accused have not been complied with, have not been given, we can at any stage exclude that from consideration. Why hold it up at this stage? Let us see in which circumstances the statement was recorded that the prosecution wants to produce before us. You see, any statement by an accused person is admissible provided what they call in England the Judges' Rules have been complied with. If the safeguards provided in the Statutes or our Rules have not been complied with, we can at any stage exclude it from consideration. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: It could not be tendered until those were complied with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We want to know the circumstances under which those statements were recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I fully understand your point, your Honour. My point is what we are holding is something akin to a voir dire on admissibility of evidence. Our submission is we should be allowed to present our evidence, call our witnesses in a trial within the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You will have the opportunity of producing your witnesses when -- we will first of all see the circumstances in which that statement was recorded. Otherwise we are just talking in the abstract. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I hope you are familiar with this type of procedure. Now when the witness comes in and claims to tender a statement, then you have the right to object and ask questions how it should be tendered. At any stage all the factors relevant to its admissibility will be raised and then if they are unable to scale that argument, that statement cannot be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I follow you completely, your Honour. The question and the problem is this: that to object to its admissibility may require the defence of Delalic to call witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: At this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes. We are asking under Rule 89(b) that you hold a hearing akin to a voir dire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: First, having taken the witness, you can object to the evidence and show that the statement of the accused is not admissible in evidence. Why at this stage do you want to lead evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Part of making that showing will involve calling witnesses on behalf of the defence. Time is needed to make arrangements for travel, to have those people here to make that showing, to issue subpoenas. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: You have not shown it is necessary at this stage. We do not know yet. Let us hear the witness and then we will know what the witness has done. That will lead us into determining whether that should be necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I am sure you are aware of the Judges' Rules apart from our own Rules here with regard to statements made by the accused on earlier occasions, although Mr Greaves did have a point: the prosecution should have indicated in the list of witnesses that this witness was to prove these statements. You are quite right. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: When I initially referred to Mr Greaves, I knew except he makes that concession, it might not be right to go forward, because there is a point that he ought to be aware and prepare for whatever is coming in. It is a witness who is coming and he should know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do not dispute that at all. I will just also, while listening to this witness, I will remind the court that there was a decision on 9th October 1996 with respect to the first interview. The prior Chamber heard evidence or reviewed the transcripts and made certain findings about compliance with the Rules. Anyway, the prosecution now calls Miss Sabine Manke. MS. SABINE MANKE (sworn) Examined by MS. McHENRY.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: May the witness be seated? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes, you can sit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Ma'am, would you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Sabine Manke.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How are you employed at the present time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I work for the Office of the Prosecutor as investigator.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to working for the Office of the Prosecutor how were you employed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a detective with the German Federal Police Force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As part of your work within the Office of the Prosecutor have you been involved in investigation into crimes alleged to have been committed in the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether or not as part of the investigation there were interviews of the accused?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all four accused were interviewed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have information concerning the manner in which these interviews were conducted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do have information, since I participated in some of the interviews, I monitored some of them and I have read all the statements that were given by the accused to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going to the accused, Mr Delalic, can you tell us when he was interviewed and where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
