utterances.text: I would need to verify with the files in Germany.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you verify at that time whether he was registered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We received information from the Federal Police Force pertaining to his person. I would need to check these files.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying that you did not personally check the German Registry of Foreign Citizens?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We are not allowed to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. To your knowledge was he registered? That is what I want to know. To your knowledge was Mr Delalic registered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would need to check the files, the correspondence with the German Police Force about this issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you had no knowledge either way whether he was registered or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have it at the moment. I would need to consult my file before I can answer your questions. If you permit me to consult the files, I can answer your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have the files in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not in this file.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we perhaps allow the witness to consult her files?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The files are in Germany probably, not here. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Actually what do you need it for?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, I want her to answer my question whether or not she knew as part of the investigations whether Mr Delalic was registered as a foreign -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: So what?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: It goes to the credibility of this witness and the thoroughness of her investigations. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I think that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In interviewing Mr Delalic did you check up whether he was registered or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not do it myself. We had to rely on the information that the German authorities provided to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What information did they supply to you in this regard, the registration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They informed us that, according to their files, Mr Delalic was registered as a resident in Munich.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right. So you are saying that you were given information that he was registered in Munich?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I didn't know whether he actually was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, all right. But that was your understanding at the time, that he was registered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The same register of foreigners would also register whether a foreigner was registered as the manager of a company, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me. The same form?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The same register of foreigners would indicate whether or not a foreigner was registered as the manager of a company, would it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what is in this register form. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: If you are sure he has business interests there and she is rightly to know that, ask her those questions and let us get to the root of it, else you will be going round and round and getting nowhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Can I, with the assistance of the usher, have a document shown to the witness, please? Excuse me. Usher, can I have your assistance, please? Can you show it to the Prosecution too, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I have no objection to that being shown to the witness. (Handed)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Miss Manke, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is dated March 6th 1996 and it is prepared by you, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is sent to Regis Abrabat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is Mr Abrabat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time he used to be my superior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of investigations here at the OTP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see the first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am looking at the English version. If you go down five lines, there is a sentence beginning with the name "Delalic". I will read it to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says: "Delalic, however, was never entered in the German Central Registry of Foreign Citizens"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. This is what I would have learned when consulting my files.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Earlier when I asked you that question you gave the opposite answer. You said he was registered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wanted to consult my files before I asked (sic) that, and this would have come out of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With all due respect, I asked you the question and you answered it in a different manner. Would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't get you, I am afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A few moments ago I asked you the same question and you gave me an opposite answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well .. in fact, you gave an opposite answer to Judge Jan's question. Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what the German authorities have communicated to me. This is what I told you. I can only tell you what they have communicated to me when consulting the files. As a result of this -- this memo you are now reading to me is a result of the information the German authorities provided us with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You know that Mr Delalic was arrested provisionally under Rule 40 of the Rules of Procedure of this Tribunal; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you know under Rule 40 the Prosecutor may request any state to arrest an individual provisionally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The basis for the provisional arrest is a case of emergency; is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you know that Mr Goldstone, the Prosecutor at that time, made such a request regarding Mr Delalic to the German authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that time there was no indictment against Mr Delalic, was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The indictment didn't come down until 21st March; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nor was there an arrest warrant from this Tribunal for Mr Delalic either, was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I considered the request which was addressed to the German authorities as a kind of arrest warrant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know Mr Schneider, the Chief Prosecutor in Munich, do you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He took necessary measures to make the provisional arrest of Mr Delalic on 18th March 1996 in Munich?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date, yes, but..

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had conversations with Mr Schneider about that arrest, didn't you, the provisional arrest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was based on your information and your investigations that that provisional fast-track arrest was made, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Could you repeat that, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You informed Mr Schneider, based on your investigations of Mr Delalic -- part of your investigations was the basis for using that Rule 40 arrest, was it not, the provisional fast-track arrest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I met with Mr Schneider to discuss the arrest, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you informed him of the results of your discussions on Mr Delalic, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Based on those two documents we've looked at here today; that was the basis for your conclusions, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The same documents that you have contradicted here on cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that it's fair to say that you've been quite personally involved in this investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Personally, if you mean emotionally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whatever. No? Okay. You know within this trial that Witness N has testified, don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, please don't mention any names, because he is a protected person, but do you know the real name of Witness N?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to show you -- because he is a protected person, to make sure we're talking about the same person, I would like to show you a piece of paper with a name on it and just tell me if we are talking about the same person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. May the prosecution see it? Thank you. No objection. (Handed to witness).

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to look at this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the name on this paper the person you know to be Witness N?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will always refer to him as Witness N then. All right. You know that Witness N has already testified in these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're familiar with what Witness N told the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you sure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Witness N was being cross-examined by my colleague, Ms Residovic, at pages 2064 and 2065 of the transcript, they were discussing statements Witness N had given to investigators and she had questions for him regarding those statements. She asked him this question: "Question: And have you met a Mrs Sabine Manke of Germany? Answer: Yes. But not linked to this?" In what way are you and Witness N linked, Miss Manke, if it's not by way of investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We met during a mission to Timisware where a number of witnesses were brought to be interviewed. I have not personally interviewed this witness but another investigator from the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us a bit about what Witness N was doing with you there and how he helped you and expand on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I have not had a chance to talk to him personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have never spoken to him personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have spoken to him personally but not at length.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but please tell us what that involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It involved his meals as a witness in Timisware. It involved his stay, accommodation, etc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you went for dinner with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it go beyond that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have no further questions, your Honour. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: That is all you have for this witness? Any other questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I have just a couple of questions in re-examination. Before that, I might ask if I could see the documents that have been shown to the witness? Re-examination by MS. McHENRY

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Miss Manke, do you have any personal relationship with Witness N? . I'm sorry I have to ask you this but I just want the record to be clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. With respect to the interview of Mr Delalic conducted in Munich can you tell us something about the circumstances under which it was suggested that Mr Delalic should have an attorney, in particular what was the purpose that Mr Hortemo suggested that Mr Delalic might wish to have an attorney?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I cannot speak for Mr Hortemo, but as far as I remember, it was the fact that we learned at this moment that Mr Delalic was to be brought before a judge around 12.30, and since this was a formal proceeding we thought it would be wise -- Mr Hortemo suggested it would be wise to have a counsel for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it correct that the questions and the suggestion as far as your information that he have an attorney had to do with the formal court proceeding that was going to happen with respect to Mr Delalic's arrest and possible subsequent transfer to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did, in fact, a lawyer come and represent Mr Delalic in the court hearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I have now remembered the name of the lawyer. It's Mr Bose, somebody from Mr Bose's law firm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't have anything else. Ma'am, are you familiar with the fact that there was a search warrant issued and certain things regarding Mr Delalic were found in March?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What has this to do with?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it has to do with the impeachment about this document. I just want to clarify particular things. I believe that some of the discussion may have had to do with misunderstandings about time, when she learned certain things versus when she wrote certain things. I think, given this attempt to the impeachment, I am allowed to just ask about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I object to that, your Honours. This re-direct is exceeding the scope of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I do not believe. It will be just one or two questions. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I do not even see how it leads to the cross-examination, because cross-examination was a specific one.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Trying to point out contradictions between what she said and what this letter represents.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Now what you are doing is getting something out of the blue which did not arise from this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: It may have been my question was too broad, because I was trying not to lead the witness. If I could be permitted one specific question, and I think that will be -- it is directly relevant to the attempted impeachment with this document, and I am referring to the document dated 19th March 1996. Let me ask you specifically, Miss Manke: among the things that were seized was there, for instance --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There was no seizure.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe I am allowed to ask her about the reason why at least as of March 19th she was able to say correctly that there were substantial and close contact with decision-makers of the Bosnian Army and that he has information about high-ranking people. That is in particular what my question is going to be devoted to. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: This is -- MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Objection, your Honour. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Now, this is the problem. The question which was asked her by counsel initially was her familiarity with the official position of Delalic in the community. She said as far as she knew there was none. Now this letter is now showing that she is targeting him as having some official position. This is a contradiction he was trying to point out.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That is exactly right, your Honour. I believe some of it may have been a misunderstanding about time. Without suggesting the answer to the witness, what I am trying to do is find out when she started the information -- she had certain information but by the time she wrote this letter on 19th March she may have had very specific knowledge in which -- which substantiates the statements in this letter. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: That is whether your question arises from the question which led to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That is correct. My question has directly -- has to do with the information that she had as of at least 19th March about substantial and close contacts with decision-makers of the Bosnian Army and authorities which was specifically put to her in cross-examination by the defence attorneys.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Well, she could have said and explained the contradictions. She could have also herself explained that while trying to explain the apparent contradictions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That is right, your Honour, but I believe that one of the purposes of re-examination is to help clarify things without leading the witness, things -- especially with the pressure of the witness stand, or because they do not believe it is being directly asked or because there is a misunderstanding. I believe that I am entitled to clarify matters raised in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You yourself have suggested the answer to her because at that time she had some limited information and later on she had more knowledge. You have already suggested the answer to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I have not, for instance, suggested what the specifics are. My first question didn't suggest anything but then I was pressed as to why I was asking it and did it fall within the scope of re-examination. I believe that I had to explain to the court why. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: The circumstances under which she made the contradiction. This is what you wanted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to clarify the attempt at impeachment. In fact, I would not agree there is necessarily a contradiction. I would at least like to attempt to clarify the attempt at impeachment. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes. Put it to her.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Ma'am, are you aware of some of the evidence that was seized from the search warrants -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: That is where the problem comes. Nobody talked about seizure of things.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Are you aware of whether or not this investigation has -- that evidence indicating that Mr Delalic had substantial and close contacts with decision-makers of the Bosnian Army and authorities was found?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you repeat this, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour. That is the same question in different clothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Ma'am, with respect to the investigation up until -- from the beginning until the present time has there been evidence suggesting that Mr Delalic had substantial and close contacts with decision-makers of the Bosnian Army and authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. If your Honours wish, I can ask her more specifically without getting into it, but I do not believe it is necessary. I just wanted to clarify that particular, but if your Honours wish me to, I can ask her more specifically?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It is going to raise some more questions like this. She is writing this letter on 19th March.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is the day when she concluded the interview. Before the interview she had certain information.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: On the basis of that she answered the questions put to her.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Was it anything in the information supplied to her by Delalic that she was able to change her opinion and say these things?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: When did the seizures take place?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: On 18th March, so it would have been -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: The letter was on 19th.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Exactly. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: That is the day after.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: The interview started on 18th March and then during 18th and 19th she learned information both from Mr Delalic and she may have learned information about the search warrants. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: You are giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am trying to respond to your question. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: No. If you can ask her points at least so that she can explain the contradiction.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Miss Manke, did you learn any information on 18th and 19th March 1996 that you did not have when the interview of Mr Delalic started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We learned an important amount of information during the interview of Mr Delalic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I have no further questions. Excuse me, your Honour. May I just double-check that? That is all, your Honour, at this point. Unless it is clear in the record, we would formally move into evidence the exhibits that this witness has testified to, the Exhibits 99. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, again with my belt and suspenders on, as long as it is not admissible against my client, I don't have any objections? I may have some if it becomes admissible against my client. In those circumstances I would like her to be subject to recall. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: We have explained the circumstances under which it could.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I think the circumstances do not exist. It remains as only evidence against the maker of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. That's why I am just being doubly careful. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, defence counsel of Zejnil Delalic is opposed to this material being accepted as evidence of the prosecution under the number recorded by the Registry. The basis for this objection is in the Decision of the Trial Chamber of 9th October 1996, during a hearing in this Chamber on 17th January 1997, and especially in Rule Number 89 of this Tribunal, 89(d), which clearly indicates that: "The Trial Chamber may exclude the submission of evidence if the need for a fair determination is more important -- is outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial". The defence is of the opinion that in the interest of a fair trial of my client it is necessary to exclude and not allow the use of this evidence in the proceedings. Rule 89 establishes that this Tribunal will not be bound by national rules of evidence but does not exclude reference to national rules. Also in sub-rule (b) it is clearly stated that the Rules must be used which will best favour a fair determination of the matter before it and are consummate with the general Statute and general principles of law. Arguing this submission, we state that on the basis of today's testimony of the witness it can also be established that while this interview was taken of the accused, Mr Delalic, his rights were seriously violated, his rights to counsel, because it is clear from the testimony of the witness that my client was only read out Rules 42 and 43, whereas the witness herself said that on the basis of her legal training and the courses she had in this Tribunal she did not have a full understanding of what the right to counsel means. The witness also said that on the list of lawyers of such a big city as Munich there was not a single lawyer who would understand and have a good knowledge of the Rules of this Tribunal. For this reason the witness confirmed that only a single lawyer was offered to my client, who had defended one of the accused before this Tribunal. The substance of Rule 21 (4) (d) is that the accused should be informed of his rights in a way that will be understandable to an ordinary person, not a trained lawyer. Clearly a simple reading of this Rule does not fulfil that requirement. It can clearly be seen from the prosecution statements that legal instructions followed only when the accused was due to appear before the court. Therefore, everything else that preceded that was not done in a way as required by the interests of a fair trial, and by Article 21 of this Tribunal. A more detailed discussion of the meaning of the right to counsel and the legal and social culture of my client who comes from a particular part of the world with a certain understanding of the role of counsel and regarding the consequences of a statement before the interrogator was clearly presented at a hearing of this Trial Chamber on January 17th. This very fact that the right to counsel was violated, in view of the prestige and the importance of this Tribunal, should be sufficient to exclude the evidence given by my client without the presence of counsel. Let me make a few more remarks. The witness today alleged that from the very beginning she was involved in the conduct of the investigations into this case. The witness recognised and confirmed that she had written a letter on March 6th. That is at a time when my client was just -- was not even a suspect or an accused, and facts were expressed that, after the prosecution intervened, urgent measures were taken towards my client. Therefore, his arrest was unlawful. Furthermore, on the basis of the facts contained in the letter of the witness of 19th are such that the results of those facts resulted in my client spending two months in solitary confinement. This witness, as well as others who interrogated my client, contrary to Rules 42 and 43 of the Rules of this Tribunal, presented themselves as interrogators of the Tribunal, which is not correct, because, in fact, they were interrogators of the prosecution. If we are talking about interrogators of the court, which are not recognised by these Rules, it is not -- they are not entitled to interview my client. The only people who are allowed to carry out interrogations are prosecutors. However, the interrogators did not introduce themselves as prosecutors, and therefore at that moment they were being unfair. Furthermore, at that moment the measures from Rule 40 were proposed to my client, which, though not contained in the Statute, should be interpreted highly restrictively, as they do not have grounds in any specific Rule of the Statute of the Tribunal. Contrary to this, Rule 40, which only envisages the right to arrest a suspect for the collection of evidence and to take all other necessary measures to prevent his escape, and for this purpose my client was interrogated without counsel, which is quite contrary to Rule 40. If the Prosecutor were to claim that he has the right to interrogate in view of the fact that he was a suspect, then he could not do so according to the provisions of Rule 40 of this Tribunal. The only possibility for the presence of the Prosecutor would be according to Rule 55(d), when there should be a warrant of arrest. There is no doubt, your Honours, that the indictment against my client was issued on 21st March, that Judge Jorda confirmed that indictment and that the arrest warrant carries that date. From that date the Prosecutor could be present at the arrest and carry out the measures envisaged by the Rules. Since from the very beginning that is the measures taken against him, the method in which the interrogators introduced themselves, the way in which the statement was taken, therefore the entire procedure was contrary to the Rules of this Tribunal, the general Rules and the rules of a fair trial in the world, and especially as this had to do with a man from a different social, cultural, legal and linguistic background, that all reasons of the defence counsel should be appreciated, so that a mini-trial could be scheduled at which the defence would confirm these allegations and invite before this Trial Chamber witnesses who would directly before the Trial Chamber confirm what we have already alleged in our motion. Therefore, our final proposal is that this evidence be excluded and that we schedule a hearing at which the defence would be able to present evidence in support of this motion. Thank you, your Honours. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: That is somewhat a confused argument. You mean we reject this evidence and then we hear it again? Let us hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I have two questions to ask from the witness. When was he arrested in Munich?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr Delalic was arrested on 18th March 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: On the very day that you interviewed him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Did you give him any notice that you were coming to interview him before interviewing him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was asked by the German police officers whether he would agree to meet investigators. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Ms McHenry, let us hear your reply.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am not sure exactly what order to give my response in. I have two basic points. One is that the investigators and everyone in the Office of the Prosecutor's Office scrupulously followed the Rules of the Tribunal and the requirements for a fair trial. That would be my first point. The second point would be that the accused -- the defence of Mr Delalic has made these exact arguments about what the requirements of a fair trial are, and whether or not different rules should apply because Mr Delalic was from a different system, and what exactly the prosecution represented in giving these rules. There was a hearing on that, and on 9th October the Trial Chamber gave a decision in which it fully considered the requirements of a fair trial, both under the Articles of the Statute, the Rules of this Tribunal, and the general requirements for a full trial, and the Trial Chamber correctly found that the Prosecutor had in all respects followed the requirements for a fair trial, for a fair interview, and that the accused had waived his right to have counsel in particular, and I do not believe that it is appropriate for the defence counsel to be permitted to raise these same arguments a second time. I believe Rule 73, which requires that these motions be brought immediately -- there are good reasons for that and, in fact, Ms Residovic did that. There was a hearing and the issue has been decided. The prosecution certainly agrees that the defence of Mr Delalic is allowed to challenge the admissibility based on whether or not the statement was fully recorded, and the court found that that would require some factual evidence, and you have heard that factual evidence, and it is that three times the tape stopped and was immediately turned over. There was no questioning that occurred that was not recorded. There has been no suggestion, no allegation, no evidence that anything improper happened in the few seconds that it required to turn the tape over, and that any attempt to state that Rule 43 was not complied with is incorrect. Going a little bit more specifically, the Rules of this Tribunal do state exactly what must be done. A reading of the entire transcript as well as this witness's testimony indicates that the accused -- every right was given to the accused. It was made sure that he understood the rights. During the interview at several times the rights were repeated. He was asked if he was sure he understood them; if he was sure he wished to waive his right to counsel. The investigator specifically read from Rule 42, which states that: "When being questioned by the Prosecutor, a suspect shall have the following rights". That was done, and that is why, your Honours, in the previous case in the October Decision this Trial Chamber found -- with different judges -- this Trial Chamber found that Rule 43 had been met in its entirety, that the accused had waived its right to counsel. It is what I can only sort of consider a bizarre situation where only because the investigator suggested to Mr Delalic more than they had to, that he should have an attorney for this legal proceeding, that it appears that we are getting into this argument. He had waived his rights and he continued to waive them. They suggested that for court he might want to have one. They made sure that until he did have one he was willing to continue the interview without an attorney. That is something that this Trial Chamber has previously found. I am not reading all the prior decision, but it states that: "Accordingly, the Trial Chamber finds that there is no violation during the conduct of this interview of the rights pursuant to sub-rule 42(a)." Then the court goes on, and the same arguments about whether or not something different needed to be done or whether or not everything -- when there was a suggestion of an attorney, that meant that the interview had to be stopped, and the court again went on to say: "It cannot be said that this interview continued in violation of sub-rule 42." With respect to Rule 43, which deals with recording, the court found that: "The defence would have to make a showing that such an irregularity in recording has led to a violation of the rights of the accused, Zejnil Delalic, that warrants the exclusion of the evidence." We submit that it is clear that there has been no violation of the rights of the accused, Mr Delalic, with respect to the recording, but the prosecution has done everything that it is required to do. In fact, it has done more than it is required to do, and it would be a miscarriage of justice for this court not to admit the statements under these circumstances. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have one point to add. There was some debate on what was the Prosecutor doing and what was an investigator doing. I would just direct your Honours's attention to Rule 37(b) where it says about the Prosecutor: "His powers under part 4-8 of the Rules may be exercised by staff members of the Office of the Prosecutor authorised by him or by any person acting under his discretion." Thank you, your Honour. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Let us hear you. Do you have anything to say? MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, the Trial Chamber, reviewing our motion, submitted, in accordance with Article 73, in connection with the interview of Mr Zejnil Delalic, the Trial Chamber decided to that purpose: ".. and in the event that the transcript is used as evidence during trial, the defence may submit an objection about its admissibility according to Rules 89 and 85. Since the transcript of that interview has still not been submitted as evidence and that the defence counsel has to prove that that material should be excluded, this motion is rejected." This Trial Chamber passed a similar decision in January this year. The Chamber did have a discussion on legal matters, but the main argument was that the motion was not submitted in a timely manner. I draw the attention of your Honours to Rule 92: "Wherefore a confession by the accused given during questioning by the Prosecutor shall, provided the requirements of Rule 63 were strictly complied with, be presumed to have been free and voluntary unless the contrary is proved". This Trial Chamber has here for the first time an investigator and a witness who showed during cross-examination that this questioning was neither correct nor fair, nor were his basic, fundamental rights envisaged by Article 21 of the Statute respected. We thank the representatives of the prosecution for giving the accused even greater rights than belonged to them. We are saying that this evidence should not be admitted, because the rights of my client were not respected according to the Statute. In response to the comment of my learned colleague, Mr Ostberg, I do not deny that in certain provisions of the Rules there is a possibility for the Prosecutor to act through its authorised representatives, and even via other states. However, the witness has confirmed that she introduced herself as an investigator and not a person authorised by the prosecution. Therefore, she incorrectly introduced herself to our client and according to our law and the rules of law in general, which Miss Manke is not familiar with, statements before the police and other authorities are not accepted in trial. To support this, let me mention that when my client was taken before the court he used his right to silence on March 19th and on 24th April in German courts, when for the first time he received an indictment in his own language, and the confirmation of that indictment as well as the warrant of arrest. Therefore, I repeat that throughout the procedure, throughout the proceedings, measures taken against my client, special measures of arrest were completely unfair, and the admission of this statement would mean to legalise the unlawful arrest and the taking of a statement at a moment when the client clearly did not understand what was read out to him. Your Honours, without the interpreters you would not understand what I am saying. When a foreigner is being read foreign rules, they are unknown to him, not because he doesn't know the law, but because he does know the law, but the law of his own country. As you said this morning, the Trial Chamber will respect the general rules of law and the general rights of the defendants, and I therefore propose that this evidence be rejected. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: The Trial Chamber will have a break now and they will return at 4.30. We will indicate then. (4.05 pm) (Short break) (4.30 pm) JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. We have considered the submissions made by counsel and we have come to the conclusion that we will admit the evidence mainly for the fact that the question of the violation of the right of the suspect under Rule 42 has not been established and it has been decided before in this Trial Chamber that there has been no violation of that right, and I think perhaps one could go further to say that those rights are rights of a suspect and they are not the rights of an accused under Article 21, and it is Rule 42 and 43 which govern the conduct of proceedings under Rule 40. Apart from that, we have not gone further to discuss the authenticity or the correctness of the video recordings and the like and that is still challenged. That will come in any time it is being played. If there is any good reason why some of the handicaps about them could lead to any prejudice to the accused person, then that can be taken up, but for the time being the defence has not shown any reason why it should not be admitted. We will give our fuller reasons later. I think I might add we discussed the question of the value of what I would regard as the weight to be attached to much of the evidence which is quite material in the circumstances in which it was taken, and the nature of the tapes themselves might be very important during cross-examination and the like. So that will also feature very largely, even though it has been admitted in evidence, because there is nothing to show that it is inadmissible. As I said, we have still decided what here was the rights of the suspects, not the rights of an accused persons. I think that is all for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: The prosecution, just for your information -- the prosecution's next witness, your Honour, would be Mr Bart d'Hooge with respect to the atatements of the other accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: It is in relation to that that I at this stage have an application to make to you. I am fully conscious that the motion that I have filed only arrived on your desks this afternoon. For that apologies, but your Honours will perhaps, knowing the circumstances in which I arrived in this case, will forgive me for that at the very least. Your Honour, the proposition that I make by that motion is this: that all evidence of that which was said by the defendant Mr Mucic to the Austrian Police and to the Office of the Prosecutor in Vienna over the period 18th March-21st March 1996 should be excluded, and if I can just give you a quick resume of the matters we say are relevant to that -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Are you sure the prosecution has already reacted to your motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I have a feeling at the very moment they are reacting on their bench, because I know they only got it just before we returned into court. Can I just carefully set out what the proposition is, so that each of my learned friends across the way know exactly what I am saying? We say that there has been a series of grave breaches of the following Rules of this Tribunal: 42(a), 42(b), the generality of Rule 43 and in particular 43(3), and that there has been a specific act of oppression by the investigator in this case, and that there are similar arguments concerning the different systems of law that were applied to this man, and he was subjected to court procedures by the Austrian courts, where the reading of his rights appears to be very different from the standard that obtains in this Tribunal, and that, as a result of those, his right to counsel was not voluntarily waived, and he did not take a properly informed decision about that. Your Honours, attached to the motion I have filed -- and can I mention, so you quickly get to the point about oppression -- were some documents. Those are documents in which the defendant, when seen by the Austrian authorities, quite clearly sets out his desire to have a lawyer. If I might just specifically refer you to them, he is seen by a lady judge at 11.05 in the morning. He says: "I want a lawyer. I hereby request that a lawyer be assigned to me. I do not have a lawyer of my own." He is seen by another judge in the afternoon at 14.20--15.20 hours and he reiterates that request. Within fifteen minutes he appears to have changed his mind as a result of a conversation which the investigator says "we have just had". That is a conversation which is not the subject of any videotape, audio-visual recording, conventional cassette recording of any kind, and it is the defence contention that during the period of that conversation this defendant was oppressed by that investigator and persuaded, effectively against his will, to do without having a lawyer. Your Honours will know that that would amount to a serious breach of the following Rules: 89(c), 89(d) and Rule 95 in particular. Your Honours have heard me refer to Rule 95 on a number of occasions. It is an important Rule. Your Honour, the process of oppression begins and can only be properly determined by viewing not just the evidence -- hearing the evidence of Mr d'Hooge, but also the prior evidence of the police officer who dealt with him, as it were, within the Austrian police part of his detention in Vienna. Can I now just take you back to the Decision in Tadic? I am sorry if I bat on about the Decision in Tadic, but it is an important one concerning, on the face of it, hearsay evidence. We say that that Decision actually applies to all evidence in this case, hearsay and other forms of evidence. In order to establish the voluntariness of this series of interviews with the defendant, the prosecution has to do three things: it has to show that it is reliable; it has to show that it is probative and relevant; and it has to show, in my submission, that it ought not to be excluded under Rule 89(d). In so doing it has, as we discussed yesterday in connection with this Decision -- it has to lay a proper foundation for reliability before it can be admitted, and in the case of a suspect who is questioned, the burden of proof lies throughout on the prosecution to prove those elements of its case. As we say that the process of oppression and this defendant being misled, effectively, about what his rights were began with the police officer who started to interview him the night before he was put before the courts in Vienna, the prosecution can only begin to found the issue of reliability by calling first Mr Morbauer, who I think is named in the list of prosecution witnesses and who was the police officer who interviewed him in Vienna, can only begin to found that by calling him first. By calling in relation to this defendant the OTP investigator first it is simply going to confuse your Honours and not enable you to take a proper decision on the issue of excluding this evidence. It can only be done in a logical, proper order, and my submission to your Honours is that that is the process that should be followed in the case of Mr Mucic, that you should not hear this witness on the interviews of Mr Mucic before you hear the police officer from Vienna, because only by doing that can a proper, informed decision on admissibility be arrived at and the Rules of the court complied with, because what it says is the prosecution has to lay its foundation properly. In our submission, it cannot do so if it approaches it in this way. I hope that is a reasonably concise setting-out of my argument. I can assist your Honours further if you need any assistance with it. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: If your main argument is that the accused was coerced into changing his mind or making certain statements, then the burden is on the prosecution to show that they did not. So they now have to show that it was his own free will and it was voluntary.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: It is going to raise a logistical problem for them, in my submission, because, because this police officer from Vienna has to start the ball rolling, it does not matter what happens in relation to the other two defendants, but, as far as my client is concerned, that evidence can only start with Mr Moerbauer. It cannot start with this officer. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes. May we hear you, Ms McHenry?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Briefly, as counsel said, the prosecution just received this motion and I think one of our main points brings up this issue, which is that the interview of Mr Mucic occurred in March of 1996. It is a requirement that counsel bring such motions within 60 days, and it is expressly so that these issues are not decided at the last minute. In April defence counsel was given a copy and transcript of Mr Mucic's interview in April of 1996, and it is now May of 1997, and this is the first that we are hearing that there is any allegation of oppression or something like this. I have, in fact, no information, although we believe the investigator should be called. We believe with respect to what happened to the Vienna Police that the interview will show that with respect to the Office of the Prosecutor interview the accused voluntarily waived his rights, and there was no unfair pressure or coercion put on him. So it is since April of 1996 that the defence has had the statements and I do not know where this allegation of oppression comes from. All I can assume is that it comes from Mr Mucic himself, in which case again I do not think there is any reason why this could not have been brought within the first 60 days. So in these circumstances we would argue that it is untimely and unfair. We believe that we should call the investigator and we believe the record will reflect that the accused voluntarily waived any rights he had without any unfair pressure or coercion being placed upon him. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Are you suggesting that if an accused person accuses your office of coercion or inducement you have no duty to establish that that was not the position.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No, your Honour, I am not suggesting that. What I am suggesting is, in fact -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: You say it is time-barred. Time can bar it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That is correct. Time can bar it. I believe that is the exact purpose of Rule 73, just to make sure that these issues are brought up before, and, for instance, in this case I will -- had this been brought up before, Mr Mucic and his counsel had agreed to be interviewed at other occasions, but, because they had no objection to the March interview, it was determined that it was not necessary. Had there been any allegation that this had been -- that there had been anything improper, his counsel -- and I had conversations with his counsel -- had indicated that he would be willing to be interviewed again. So I think it is very unfair. I do certainly believe when your Honours hear this witness they will be in a position to find that the accused -- that the statement is admissible also, because, in fact, we believe that. So there are two separate arguments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Which is the relevant Rule you are referring to, 73? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I think the accusation is against a particular witness, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just now a distinction has been drawn between a suspect and an accused. Rule 73 applies: "Exclusion of evidence obtained from the accused". It does not use the word "suspect". The limitation would apply to that. Read that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You must have heard the learned Presiding Judge drawing the distinction between a suspect and an accused.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, but I believe in this case it is clear that "accused" means -- there are only accused and the Rules always refer to accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The Rules refer to suspects and accused and there is a distinction drawn between them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That's right but with respect to preliminary motions by an accused, a person will only be accused --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Exclusion of evidence obtained from the accused, not a suspect. You have just heard the distinction being drawn between accused and suspect?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I understand your argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It is just an observation, not an argument.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. I understand the observation, but the prosecution would contend that "accused" in this case refers to preliminary motions by accused, and that if someone -- if evidence is seized from someone at the time they are a suspect and they subsequently become an accused, Rule 73 applies. I note in the prior Decision by this Trial Chamber of October that we were referring to it is exactly the same position, and the court did find Rule 73 applicable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I was just drawing your attention to the distinction just drawn.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, I see your point. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Anxiety is mainly in the fundamental nature of the contention. If someone is contending that he did not make a statement voluntarily, it might not be in the interests of justice to exclude that contention. It might be very detrimental to the administration of justice for one to exclude it merely because it was not raised in time, because it is fundamental to the defence as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, your Honour, I certainly, for instance, believe that all the rights in Rule 73, including jurisdiction, the most basic of the rights -- I believe that they are fundamental rights and there is nothing in what the prosecution is saying that suggests that the voluntariness of a confession or of a statement is not a fundamental right. We would certainly agree with that, but we would contend that Rule 73 states that such fundamental issues, because they are in part so important to the case, must be brought within 60 days unless good cause can be shown. I think that is necessary so that there can be justice for both sides and that this court can find the truth. Now, in fact, let me be very clear. We have no information whatsoever to suggest that the statement is not voluntary, and we believe that we will be able to establish that, but -- so in the event your Honours were to consider waiving this right, we believe we will be able to show it, although I do not know the specifics exactly of even what Mr Greaves is talking about, which is, I think, another reason why Rule 73 requires that these things be made within the first 60 days, absent a showing of good cause. Given that the statements were provided to the accused in April of 1996, immediately after he was brought to The Hague, we do not believe there has been any showing of that. MS. TAPUSKOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, if you allow me to respond to the learned colleague McHenry, I do have to say yes, this opportunity did exist in April of 1996, but the defence team that is sitting at this bench today was not there at that time. We have a responsibility to Mr Mucic as of the date of our appointment. We do not want to speculate on what could have happened and been at that time. Rule 73(c) points out the failure to apply within the time limit prescribed constitutes a waiver of the right. However, it further says: "The Trial Chamber may grant relief from the waiver upon the showing of good cause." This is exactly what we are trying to do. We are trying to point to good cause. Why do we do that? We do not want to bring this Rule 73(c) -- bring in through the back door. There are in these very Rules -- they give us the opportunity to not present certain evidence before this Trial Chamber. In Tadic Judge McDonald said that unfortunately the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of this Tribunal only contain ten provisions regarding the evidence. In other words, she pointed to a certain paucity of the Rules governing the presentation of evidence. However, in this present case we have enough provisions. We, that is the defence of Mr Mucic, are trying to show that the statements that the Prosecutor is trying to introduce here, which are the statements given to the Vienna Police and to the investigators of this Tribunal, have not been produced in a way proper -- based on the Rules of this Tribunal, then that constitutes good cause that allows us to file a motion pursuant to Rule 73, and the Trial Chamber has the right to rule on this, and withdraw and annul the waiver of rights of the accused, and I do also point to the difference between the suspect and the accused in these rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: May I respond just very briefly, your Honour? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes, you may respond.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have all the respect for my learned opposing counsel with respect to the accused Mr Mucic, but this brings up -- the argument being made here is the argument that is sort of continually made, which appears to be whenever new counsel comes along and makes a different strategy decision, that somehow constitutes good cause, and the prosecution is very troubled by this suggestion, especially given the continuing changes in defence counsel. The prosecution has tried and has not interfered with the accused and the relationship with their defence counsel. It is not our business and we do not want to interfere, but we are unable to accept the idea that whenever new counsel comes along and does not like a prior Decision, especially with the benefit of hindsight, that that constitutes good cause, particularly when we are two months into trial. I think it is very unfair. I would also point out that although as of now at least Mr Tapuskovic was appointed counsel in July of 1996, I believe that even if there had been some argument that first counsel, Mr Rhodes -- that the 60 days should not apply to him, in fact, I believe -- I am not positive of this -- in fact, Judge McDonald had specifically given new counsel appointed in July 1996 an additional 60 days to bring motions under Rule 73. So I -- the prosecution both with respect to this accused and with respect to other accused thinks the argument that new counsel has come is not good cause.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can I pose this question for my learned friend to answer? If there is a prima facie case that I can demonstrate through the paper that I have served on the court that there is a proper argument that there was not a voluntary waiver of counsel, would she say it was fair to deprive him entirely in this trial of an opportunity to litigate that matter? How does she answer that question, please? MS. TAPUSKOVIC (in interpretation): If you will allow me, your Honours, to address you one more time, I think that the answer of the Prosecutor that we received now would have been the same in July in 1996 had our client filed the same motion. We are -- those are not our arguments, though. The introduction of this evidence has only come up now and so this is why these arguments are coming up. Whenever previous attempts have been made to do this, the responses, and not just to this counsel but to the counsel of all four of the accused -- the answer was that this will be argued when these questions arise. These questions have now arisen. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you very much for your arguments. Actually we have looked at the Rules. In determining what is a good cause I think sometimes through the weight of the argument itself and some other surrounding circumstances -- perhaps the prejudice against an accused person might be more if it was not allowed might be a strong reason for accepting the argument as a good cause for waiving whatever exclusionary provision there is. I think in these circumstances it is necessary to waive the 60-day Rule and allow them to argue it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, your Honour. I have a more fundamental problem on this witness. When my client was interviewed twice there were as best I can determine five people in the room. The defendant himself, an interpreter, Mr d'Hooge, Mr Karabdic and Ms McHenry, and it is conceivable that the two lawyers could be witnesses on the admissibility of this. I do not think it would be proper for Mr Karabdic to be handling this as an attorney, but at the same time as a potential -- because he is a potential witness and that goes for all of the lawyers that were sitting in that room when these statements were taken, because there is the potential risk that they might be -- either Ms McHenry or Mr Karabdic may be a witness on the issue of admissibility and I want to bring that to the court's attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have filed yesterday, taking perhaps a different tack from my co-counsel, from my reading of Rule 73, a motion for an extension of time in which I could file a motion under Rule 73 to enquire into the admissibility of my client's statement. Rule 73, among other things, has some internal inconsistency that could make it operate in the very harshest of fashions. Rule 73 says that the motions must be made within 60 days of one's initial appearance, so that if one made an initial appearance and his statement was taken 61 days later, under this Rule he would never be able to challenge it, and, in fact -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I thought statements could be even taken after initial appearance?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The Chamber has already decided to waive the time bar. Why are you arguing these points.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: 73 then goes out of your way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I am sorry. I thought that was only with respect to Mr Mucic? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: No, definitely what you are saying, even if you argue that a statement could be taken after initial appearance, usually statements have been taken before initial appearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In the case of Mr Landzo it was not. It was taken 30 days after the initial appearance, leaving him 30 days within which to file his challenge under the Rule.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If I may be heard, your Honour, we do not disagree that there might be some situations where a statement is taken after 60 days and we would certainly believe that that could constitute good cause and we would never be in a position to argue otherwise. With respect to the waiver of Rule 73, I understand that your Honours have ruled, because of the specific allegations made by Mr Greaves, which are so serious, that Rule 73 -- that you are waiving the requirements of Rule 73. I believe the situation with Mr Landzo and the reasons that he seeks to waive Rule 73 are entirely different, and that we would wish to be briefly heard on why, certainly with respect to Mr Landzo, there should not be any waiver of Rule 73, since there is no -- since there is no similar allegations. In fact, Mr Landzo was represented by counsel during his interview. So if you would like me to briefly respond now, I can do that. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Actually when I made the Ruling, I stated very clearly that the grounds for seeking a waiver would determine whether it could be granted or not, whether it could be a good cause. If it is so serious that there will be substantial prejudice to the accused person, definitely the exclusionary provisions could not apply. This is what I stated. Now if you give other reasons which are not as weighty as that, perhaps one might think twice. It is not a matter of applying a soft cause. If you have to give good cause, as 73 says, you have to show good cause, and good cause does not necessarily mean any cause which perhaps you think is satisfactory to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe I understand what you have said and your reasons for waiving it with respect to Mr Mucic, but, for exactly the reasons you say, that the allegations of what the good cause is and the allegations of what rights have been violated, may affect the balancing process of what constitutes good cause. We do not believe, with respect to Mr Landzo, that there can be any argument that good cause exists, and we would like to be heard on that particular issue with respect to Mr Landzo. I understand that your Honours have ruled with respect to Mr Mucic, based on why he claims good cause.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just because I promised the court earlier this morning I would file something, I have filed something based on the court's Ruling earlier today and I do not think that either the Trial Chamber or the prosecution has it to hand. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes. Let us hear Mr Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a proposal for the court, a suggestion for the court, if I may. I filed my motion yesterday. If the prosecution even has it yet, I do not know?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: We have and we are able to respond now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Mr Moran apparently just filed a motion today. Many of the issues are similar and it is now after 5 o'clock on Friday. Might I suggest that the prosecution and all the parties have the time between now and the next time the court sits to ponder these issues and be prepared to make our arguments a lot more precise and a lot more effectively to the court and then the court could decide them at that time. In addition, the court would have the benefit of that time to look at all the papers that have been filed and consider the matter carefully. That is my proposal. Thank you. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: It is a very thoughtful proposal. I think it is a good idea. I have not read your paper at all. I have not read the motion. Neither have I seen Mr Moran's motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, again I apologise for the lateness. It's explained, I think, in the papers. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I suppose the next hearing date I think will be on Wednesday next week, because we will not be sitting on Monday or Tuesday. So we should be able to look at it afresh. If you have any reasons why you should change your mind, you can do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I understand. If I could just ask with respect to Mr Mucic, for who good cause has been raised, either now or immediately after court if Mr Greaves could indicate to us exactly what the oppression, alleged oppression was, I think that might enable us to more productively use the remaining time to look into what is a serious allegation. In the motion of Mr Greaves it does not say anything, so either here in open court or immediately afterwards I think it would only -- it is fair to the prosecution to be at least given some idea of the specifics of this, so we can try to examine the matter. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I remember his mentioning an Austrian police officer who caused the accused person to change his mind within a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Of course I will do what I can to assist my learned friend. That is only fair for me to do that. It is on this condition, though, that nothing of what I say to her is communicated to the witness in question, because I do not wish to alert him so that he can make up an answer to the question when it comes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I do not think that the prosecution can adhere to such a suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: There is a real danger that if the prosecution discuss what I am about to tell them, that the witness will be alerted to what has happened, and it would not be the first time in a court of criminal law that a witness who has been alerted to an allegation that has been made against him spends the next five days thinking up how he is going to deal with it and get round it. It would be grossly unfair if the witness was given an opportunity to go away and think of what he is going to do to answer it. That is my submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases, if I may respond to that, why should Mr Greaves have the benefit of surprise, attack a witness and bring allegations so grave that the Chamber has found grounds to waive their 60 days rule. I cannot see that. I think it would be fair to the prosecution and even to our coming witness to know what all this is about. I cannot see why we should have surprise allegations in the court room. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I do not know what you regard as a surprise here. The general allegation is one of oppression. The content of the oppression is what I do not know. That is what he is keeping to himself. The accused person who was oppressed or coerced into changing his view. That is what he said. If you want to know the details of the oppression, that is a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: It may be naive of me but I had always rather thought that all cross-examination was supposed to be a surprise to witnesses. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Well, I know he has to be told -- he must have mentioned the name of the particular witness who you are expecting to be invited to defend this and then he knows there is an allegation of oppression against him. If it is true, then he should know what type of transaction transferred between himself and the accused.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. At this point we are not even sure who the allegation is against. Is it the witness who is coming or is it against the Austrian police officer? I have to say we don't even understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I thought he made the allegation against the investigator. He said: why should the accused change his mind when twice he appeared before a judge saying: "I want a counsel." Then something happened between the investigator and the accused and the accused then suddenly says: "All right. I waive my right." I think this was the allegation which Mr Greaves may have had.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour has got it in one.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: The Office of the Prosecutor investigator?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Actually I thought it was very straightforward and clear. I did not see this confusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am sorry for my confusion but I was confused. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you very much, ladies and gentlemen. I think that is the end of the proceedings for the day. We will meet on Wednesday, 14th so that we can have these matters discussed. Thank you. (5.15 pm)
